title: FAA Rolled Out New AI Traffic Tool Right Before Nationwide Ground Stop
content:
CNN Aviation Analyst Says ‘It’s Just Too Much of a Coincidence’ FAA Rolled Out New AI Traffic Tool Right Before Nationwide Ground Stop
“It’s just too much of a coincidence” that the FAA rolled out a new $875 million AI tool meant to assist in managing air traffic the same day the United States experienced a nationwide ground stop, said CNN aviation analyst Mary Schiavo Friday.
Schiavo, the former Inspector General of the United States Department of Transportation, said:
I’ll read right from their press release, their new artificial intelligence tool called SMART, to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system, and it says it won’t affect safety. It’s called strategic management of airspace routing systems, and of course, we need new systems. But many times in the past, what we have seen, and this has gone back decades, is that because air traffic control is this piecemeal, mishmash of a whole bunch of different systems, and just as Pete said, some going back to radio, telephones and floppy disks, but when they put in new computer systems, they often have difficulty talking with communicating with or working with the much older systems.
And I have to say, it’s a tremendous amount of coincidence that right now, I mean, that they announced that they were going to start doing this, particularly since one of the goals of the SMART system — it’s not that we don’t need this — we need this. But one of the goals of the SMART system was to manage the en route traffic.
“And so if they’re putting in new software now, this new SMART system, to start managing that. And now we have a communications outage,” she added. “We’ve seen this so many times in the past. I don’t know if they’re linked, but it’s just too much of a coincidence that they’re trying to start that moving today, and now we have problems with the en route system.”
Schiavo also pointed out that there haven’t been any suggestions that the stoppage is due to “threats or criminal terror.” She added, “We haven’t heard anything like that. So I am guessing that once again we have a problem with new air traffic control computer systems, artificial intelligence. You know, modern systems, trying to communicate with old systems.”
Watch the above via CNN.

report.summary: The FAA's $875M AI airspace tool SMART launched the same day a nationwide communications outage triggered a ground stop, prompting expert suspicion but no confirmed link.
report.background: The FAA has spent decades layering new technology on top of legacy air traffic control infrastructure — some of it still reliant on copper lines, radio relays and floppy-disk-era systems. The agency's modernization push, from the NextGen program onward, has repeatedly run into integration problems where new software struggles to talk to older subsystems. The newly announced SMART system (Strategic Management of Airspace Routing Systems), reported at roughly $875 million, is designed to help manage en route traffic across the national airspace, part of a broader government-wide push to embed AI in federal operations. Aviation safety experts have long warned that the riskiest moment in any modernization effort is cutover — when new automation begins interacting with the fragmented, aging systems controllers actually depend on. The FAA has also faced recent high-profile outages and radar disruptions, sharpening scrutiny of its technical resilience.
key_points: The timing is the story: the FAA's SMART AI tool was announced as going live the same day a communications failure halted flights nationwide. Former DOT Inspector General Mary Schiavo called the overlap 'just too much of a coincidence,' while stressing that no link has been confirmed and there is no indication of a cyberattack or terror threat.

SMART is aimed at en route traffic — the high-altitude cruise phase managed by regional air traffic control centers. That is precisely the layer that appeared to fail during the outage, which is why analysts see the overlap as noteworthy rather than merely coincidental.

The core theory is legacy integration, not AI sentience. Schiavo and others argue the recurring pattern is new computer systems failing to interoperate with decades-old radios, phone lines and aging mainframes — a known failure mode in past FAA upgrades.

The price tag invites scrutiny: $875 million is a large bet on unproven automation layered onto infrastructure that controllers already describe as a patchwork, and FAA insists the tool does not affect safety margins.

No evidence yet exists either way. Officials have not attributed the ground stop to SMART, and the coincidence remains a hypothesis floated by analysts on cable news — a reminder that early explanations for aviation incidents are often wrong.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a cautionary tale about deploying automation into safety-critical legacy environments, where the bottleneck is interoperability rather than model quality. Vendors pitching AI to government will face harder questions about cutover testing, rollback plans and graceful degradation. For developers, the lesson is unglamorous but durable: integration with old systems causes more failures than algorithms do, and observability plus fallback paths matter more than benchmarks. For travelers and the public, the practical effect is likely tighter oversight and more disclosure around major aviation IT changes, plus heightened suspicion that any future outage will be blamed on the newest system in the room — fairly or not. Expect congressional questions on the SMART timeline and testing record.
report.tools: To follow the technical thread, look at the BlueSky open-source air traffic simulator from TU Delft for modeling en route operations, and the OpenSky Network or ADS-B Exchange for crowd-sourced live flight and radar data. OpenAP provides an open aircraft performance model useful for traffic simulations. NASA's FACET and the FAA's public SWIM data feeds offer insight into real airspace flow management. For AI-in-safety-critical-systems context, watch NIST's AI Risk Management Framework and EUROCONTROL publications on automation in air traffic management.
